title: Was the NFL’s Week 1 Scoring Boom a Fluke — or a Sign of Things to Come?
subtitle: The league opened 2026 with a historic scoring binge, and NFL offenses only tend to get better from here. 😳
contentHtml:
If there was a word to describe Week 1 of the NFL season, it was: “Offensive.”

Subscribe now

Led by the Chicago Bears putting up 59 points — tied for the second-most by a team on opening week since the 1970 AFL merger — against the Carolina Panthers (who themselves scored 37), teams went into Monday Night Football on track for the highest-scoring Week 1 in post-merger history (25.0 points per-team, per-game), having produced the third-highest-scoring NFL Sunday specifically in that span (26.7 PPG),1 along with one of the three-dozen or so highest-scoring single weeks in post-merger history overall.

Sundays, fundays

Along the way, more individual records were challenged, such as the most separate players scoring at least 1 touchdown and/or multiple TDs and/or 3+ TDs in Week 1. (Derrick Henry, always one of my favorites, being among that latter group — whoa!)

Famously, Week 1 of the NFL season is the epicenter of all media overreactions in maybe all of sports. Our amount of actual current-season data has just increased infinitely relative to what we had before — which is to say, zero data — and we probably did learn something from it… but there’s a LOT of noise in that signal. Most of what we think we’ve figured out this week is going to just end up being bullshit, and we have to make our peace with that.

But what I’m interested in, coming out of this high-scoring opening week, is where things will go from here. Outliers like “the highest-scoring opening week ever” scream out for regression to the mean — but there are also factors pointing in a different direction.

Most years, the NFL season is not like a baseball game: In MLB, the first inning is generally the highest-scoring inning, for reasons that vary from the top of the order getting guaranteed plate appearances to pitchers needing to settle in early in a game. But in the NFL schedule, it’s usually the offenses that need to settle in more at first. Back when the league had 17-week schedules from 1990-2020,2 Week 1 tended to see 2.3 percent less scoring (i.e., per-team PPG) than the average week in a season; since the league’s expansion to 18-week seasons in 2021,3 Week 1 has been down even further, at -3.1 percent relative to the typical week.

When does scoring tend to pick up, then? Here’s the typical increase/decrease in team PPG each week, relative to the eventual season average, for both the 17-week and 18-week eras:

Scoring generally picks up after the early weeks

Under the old 17-week setup, Weeks 1-3 were uniformly down in terms of average scoring, with points only beginning to pick up from Week 4 onward (before falling again in the last few weeks of the schedule). That was a 29-year sample size, of course; things have been a bit more all over the place in the five years since the 18-week schedule became implemented, with much less of a clear pattern around when scoring spikes or drop-offs occur. (Week 8 is apparently a big boom for scoring, but Weeks 6-7 and 9-12 aren’t, for some reason.)

But both samples can agree that scoring does tick upward from Week 1 versus the full season overall. And if that ends up being true again in 2026… well, the defenses, and the scoreboards, are about to take a massive beating.

Of course, there are plenty of theories we can put out into the void for why this scoring explosion happened, from defenses not having a real preseason (i.e., one anybody would take seriously) to use as preparation for the year, to offenses finally figuring out how to beat some of the tactics that had slowed them down earlier in the decade.4

Or maybe Week 1 of the 2026 campaign was just weird. It’s not something we’ll know either way for, well, 17 more weeks. But it does put scoring more under the microscope as we look ahead to Week 2. If the points keep piling up, this past Sunday will look like a harbinger of scorefests to come. If not, it would not only be a break with the general rule of recent NFL history — that offenses only get better after their opening warm-up — but also your annual reminder that Week 1 mainly exists just to make us all look foolish.

1

Excluding Sunday, December 25, 2011 — which only had one game on it because of Christmas.

2

With one exception, 1993, which was an 18-week schedule that gave teams TWO bye weeks apiece (a concept that was quickly shelved). Also, an important note for the data here: I’m actually dropping 2020 from this sample as well, since it was disrupted by the Covid pandemic on multiple levels (including no preseason at all, no fans at games, and many rescheduled games). I figured it would be best to keep it out of the analysis.

3

Obviously excluding 2026, since we don’t know what the eventual regular-season PPG level will be this year.

4

Yes, we are now more than halfway done with the decade of the 2020s. WHAT???
